question: It can be difficult to set goals for a team that are challenging, yet achievable. Tell me about a time when you hit the right balance. How did you approach setting the goals? What was the outcome?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project I owned the on-call rotation metrics. I set a goal to reduce P99 latency by 15% in one quarter after talking to my mentor about what was realistic given the current baseline of 800ms.
How did you decide on 15%?
I looked at the last two quarters of data, factored in the two new instances we were adding, and checked with the senior engineer on the team. We hit 17% reduction.
What would you have done if you missed it?
I would have written up what slowed us down and adjusted the next quarter's target based on that.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you set challenging yet achievable goals
Candidate owned individual on-call metrics project
Used prior data + mentor input to pick 15% P99 reduction target
Hit 17%; described fallback plan if missed
Follow-up: How did you decide on 15%? → data + senior check
Follow-up: What if missed? → post-mortem and adjust next quarter
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Deliver Results for junior level. The candidate described owning an individual metric, using historical data and a quick mentor check to land on a 15% P99 reduction target, then delivering 17%. Quote: 'I looked at the last two quarters of data, factored in the two new instances.' This shows appropriate scope, coachability, and a simple learning loop. The lower answer below sets a goal with no data or review and treats the outcome as luck. Biggest gap in weak answers is absence of any method to choose the target.

lowerTranscript.text: My manager told me to improve the dashboard load time so I said we'd do it by 20% that quarter.
How did you pick 20%?
It just sounded like a good stretch number. We ended up at 8% because other work came up.
What did you learn?
That goals can be hard to hit when priorities shift.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you set challenging yet achievable goals
Goal handed down as 'improve dashboard'
Picked 20% because 'it sounded like a good stretch'
Missed at 8% due to shifting priorities
Follow-up: How did you pick 20%? → no data or review
Follow-up: What did you learn? → goals are hard when priorities change
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Deliver Results for junior level. The candidate accepted a vague goal, chose 20% with no supporting data or input, and missed at 8% while attributing it only to 'shifting priorities.' Quote: 'It just sounded like a good stretch number.' This shows no ownership of the target-setting process and no attempt to adjust or learn from the miss. The strong answer above used data and a mentor to set a calibrated target and described a concrete fallback.

raiseTranscript.text: Last year I led a cross-team effort to cut API error rate from 1.2% to 0.4%. I pulled baseline data from three services, ran a quick planning session with the owning teams, and landed on the 0.4% target after modeling the two biggest error sources.
How did you get the other teams to commit?
I showed them the shared customer impact and offered to take the first two fixes myself to prove the approach.
What was the result?
We hit 0.35% in six months and the model became the template for two other services.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you set challenging yet achievable goals
Led cross-team API error reduction from 1.2% to 0.4%
Used multi-service data + joint planning session to set target
Influenced without authority by taking first fixes
Hit 0.35%; model reused by two other teams
Follow-up: How did you get commitment? → showed impact + offered to lead
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Deliver Results for senior level. The candidate drove a cross-team goal, used data from three services to set a 0.4% error target, and secured buy-in by taking early work themselves. Quote: 'I showed them the shared customer impact and offered to take the first two fixes.' They delivered 0.35% and created a reusable model. The lower answer sets an arbitrary team goal with no cross-team coordination or measurement. Biggest gap in weak answers is lack of influence or measurable outcome beyond the candidate's own team.

lowerTranscript.text: I told my team we needed to improve reliability and set a goal of 99.9% uptime for the quarter.
Did other teams need to help?
A little, but I mostly tracked it myself and we landed around 99.7%.
How did you choose 99.9%?
It matched what I had seen at my last company.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you set challenging yet achievable goals
Set 99.9% uptime goal for own team
No data or cross-team input on target
Landed at 99.7%; tracked mostly alone
Follow-up: Did other teams help? → minimal involvement
Follow-up: How did you choose 99.9%? → copied from prior company
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Deliver Results for senior level. The candidate set a 99.9% uptime target with no supporting data or cross-team alignment and delivered 99.7% while doing most tracking alone. Quote: 'It matched what I had seen at my last company.' This shows no attempt to influence beyond the immediate team or to calibrate the goal to current reality. The strong answer above used multi-team data and secured commitments to hit a measurable cross-team outcome.

raiseTranscript.text: When I took over the platform team we were shipping on time but with high defect rates. I worked with each engineer to set individual goals tied to a team target of 30% fewer Sev-1 incidents while still meeting the roadmap.
How did you handle the engineers who pushed back?
Two engineers thought the target was too aggressive so I paired them with a senior to review their first two quarters of incidents and let them propose the final number.
What happened?
Incidents dropped 34% and the two engineers later used the same approach on their own projects.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you set challenging yet achievable goals
Set team target of 30% fewer Sev-1s while protecting roadmap
Co-created goals with each engineer; handled pushback by letting them propose final number
Delivered 34% reduction; two engineers later reused the method
Follow-up: How did you handle pushback? → data review + let them set final target
Follow-up: Outcome? → 34% drop and method spread
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Deliver Results for manager level. The candidate set a team-wide 30% Sev-1 reduction goal while protecting the roadmap, then worked one-on-one with engineers to create ownership. Quote: 'I paired them with a senior to review their first two quarters of incidents and let them propose the final number.' The team hit 34% and the approach spread. The lower answer imposes a top-down goal without addressing underperformance or building team capability. Biggest gap in weak answers is treating goal setting as a manager-only exercise.

lowerTranscript.text: I set a team goal to reduce incidents by 25% and tracked it in our weekly meeting.
What did you do when two people weren't contributing?
I reminded them in the meeting and the number ended up at 18%.
Did you adjust the goal?
No, I kept the same target for the next quarter.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you set challenging yet achievable goals
Announced 25% incident reduction goal
Tracked in weekly meeting; no individual ownership
Hit 18%; no adjustment after miss
Follow-up: What about non-contributors? → public reminder only
Follow-up: Did you adjust? → kept same target next quarter
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Deliver Results for manager level. The candidate announced a 25% incident reduction goal, tracked it publicly, and accepted 18% without coaching or adjustment. Quote: 'I reminded them in the meeting.' This shows no development of individuals or ownership of team outcomes. The strong answer above created per-engineer goals, handled resistance by building ownership, and saw the method spread beyond the original goal.

raiseTranscript.text: Two years ago our business unit was missing revenue targets because of unreliable fulfillment. I set a three-year org goal to reach 99.5% fulfillment accuracy while growing volume 40%, then broke it into annual operating plan targets with clear trade-off decisions on where to invest.
How did you decide the 40% volume growth was compatible?
I modeled three scenarios with Finance and Ops and picked the middle path that required two new automation projects but no headcount increase.
What was the outcome after year one?
We hit 99.2% accuracy and 38% volume growth; the model is now used for the next two business units.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you set challenging yet achievable goals
Set three-year org goal: 99.5% fulfillment accuracy + 40% volume growth
Modeled three scenarios with Finance/Ops to choose feasible path
Required two automation projects, no headcount increase
Year one: 99.2% accuracy, 38% growth; model reused
Follow-up: How did you validate compatibility? → scenario modeling with partners
Follow-up: Year-one result? → near miss and org reuse
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Deliver Results for exec level. The candidate set a multi-year org goal linking 99.5% fulfillment accuracy to 40% volume growth, then used cross-functional modeling to pick an achievable path that avoided headcount. Quote: 'I modeled three scenarios with Finance and Ops and picked the middle path.' Year one delivered 99.2% and 38% growth with the approach spreading. The lower answer sets a stretch target with no strategic modeling or trade-off analysis. Biggest gap in weak answers is absence of long-term leverage or business-level calibration.

lowerTranscript.text: I told the organization we needed to hit 99.9% fulfillment next year because customers expect it.
Did you model the volume impact?
We assumed the existing teams could absorb the growth.
What actually happened?
Accuracy reached 99.4% but volume only grew 12% because of capacity issues.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you set challenging yet achievable goals
Set 99.9% fulfillment target for the org
No modeling of volume or capacity trade-offs
Hit 99.4% accuracy but only 12% volume growth
Follow-up: Did you model volume impact? → assumed teams could absorb
Follow-up: What happened? → missed volume due to capacity
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Deliver Results for exec level. The candidate set a 99.9% fulfillment target with no scenario modeling or capacity trade-offs and delivered 99.4% accuracy at the cost of only 12% volume growth. Quote: 'We assumed the existing teams could absorb the growth.' This shows no strategic judgment on long-term feasibility or leverage. The strong answer above used multi-year modeling and cross-functional input to set a goal that balanced accuracy and growth.

diagnostic.junior: Uses data + mentor input vs arbitrary number
diagnostic.senior: Cross-team data + joint planning vs copied from prior role
diagnostic.manager: Co-creates with engineers vs top-down announcement
diagnostic.exec: Multi-year scenario modeling with partners vs assumption-based

diagnostic.junior: Describes fallback adjustment vs no plan
diagnostic.senior: Offers early work to build buy-in vs minimal coordination
diagnostic.manager: Pairs for ownership vs public reminders only
diagnostic.exec: Chooses feasible path after trade-offs vs no capacity analysis

diagnostic.junior: Individual metric improvement vs vague team goal
diagnostic.senior: Cross-team reuse of approach vs single-team result
diagnostic.manager: Method spreads to other engineers vs no development
diagnostic.exec: Org-level model adopted elsewhere vs isolated miss on volume

diagnostic.junior: Baseline + new capacity factored in vs stretch number chosen for sound
diagnostic.senior: Three-service baseline + modeling vs prior-company benchmark
diagnostic.manager: Individual goals tied to team target vs one number for all
diagnostic.exec: Three scenarios with Finance/Ops vs single stretch target
